short: In 23 BCE Augustus traded the consulship for tribunician power and an authority senior to any governor's, the lasting basis of imperial rule.
full:
On 1 July 23 BCE, having held the consulship every year since 31 BCE, Augustus resigned it, answering unease at his permanent grip on Rome's senior magistracy. In its place the Senate voted him tribunicia potestas for life, giving him a tribune's sacrosanctity, veto and right to convene assemblies without ever standing for the office, and imperium proconsulare maius, a proconsular command explicitly superior to any provincial governor's, even outside his own provinces.

The change freed the consulship for senatorial competition, easing a real grievance, without touching Augustus's actual authority. From this point emperors dated their reigns by successive years of tribunician power rather than by consulships held, a convention that lasted throughout the imperial period. More than the first, the Second Settlement fixed the constitutional shape the Principate kept for two centuries.
